solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Tropical fruit always eaten by dad

indicators.note: a thing eaten by another ends up inside it, so the first piece goes within the second

parts.note: papa is a child's word for dad
ay (or aye) is an old poetic word for always

explanation.surface: A father wolfing down some exotic fruit at every opportunity.
explanation.walkthrough: AY for 'always' survives mainly in verse and in 'for ay'.
explanation.definitionFit: The papaya is a large orange-fleshed fruit grown in the tropics.

clue.text: Weapon of old station workers

parts.note: to station troops is to quarter them, lodge them at a post
the workers of a firm are its staff

explanation.surface: Railway station employees of the past carrying some antique weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of old' belongs with the definition: the weapon is a historical one, not the station.
explanation.definitionFit: A long iron-tipped wooden pole was a common fighting implement for English peasants in medieval times.

clue.text: Argument can end in dismissal, I'm sure

parts.note: can and quod are both British slang for prison

indicators.note: the end in a word is its final letter, taken from the word that follows

parts.note: 'I bet' is a way of saying 'I'm sure'

explanation.surface: Someone confident that a dispute will finish with a sacking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a verb but is the slang noun for jail; QUOD is old British slang for the same.
explanation.definitionFit: In medieval scholastic philosophy this was a debate or disputation on a freely chosen theological or philosophical point.

clue.text: Sour beer turned into average lager

indicators.note: turned means the letters picked out are then read backwards
into says the letters lie within the words average lager, across the gap

explanation.surface: A pint of ordinary lager that has gone off and become sour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' finds RAGELA spanning 'average lager'; 'turned' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: This is malt vinegar, made from ale that has soured, much as vinegar comes from wine.

clue.text: Would they invoke bad for something better?

indicators.note: bad suggests the words are spoiled and in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Wondering why anyone would call on evil in hope of improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges WOULD THEY INVOKE. The definition is the phrase that follows 'better' in the proverb 'better the devil you know (than the devil you don't)'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says a familiar evil beats an unknown one, so this phrase is what is 'better'.

clue.text: Investigate crashed cars here

indicators.note: cars that have crashed are wrecked and broken up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A police instruction to look into a scene of vehicle collisions.
explanation.definitionFit: To research a subject is to study and look into it systematically.

clue.text: Tidy up old vehicles

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means the word is written from bottom to top, read backwards

parts.note: smart means neat and tidy in appearance

explanation.surface: An instruction to clean up some ancient vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tidy up' reads as one verb phrase, but 'Tidy' is an adjective giving SMART and 'up' turns it over.
explanation.definitionFit: Trams are streetcars running on rails, largely a thing of the past in many British cities.

clue.text: Like ice, sparkle on the house?

parts.note: something on the house is given free of charge
zing is liveliness or sparkle

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a complimentary sparkling drink comes as cold as ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the house' is not a positional indicator: it is a phrase meaning free, placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice is formed by water freezing, and very cold things are described as freezing.

clue.text: Kid given posh pasta sauce

parts.note: to kid someone is to tease or rag them
U is the crossword abbreviation for upper-class, posh

explanation.surface: A child being served an upmarket sauce for their pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child but is the verb to tease.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragu is an Italian meat-based sauce eaten with pasta, as in ragu alla bolognese.

clue.text: Bats and elves trapped?

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: Fanciful image of flying mammals and little folk caught in a snare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the creatures but is the adjective meaning mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone enslaved is held captive in bondage, loosely trapped, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Dressed in black and very mature

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black on pencils
aged means very old, very mature

explanation.surface: An elderly person dressed all in black.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressed' means a wound has been dressed, not clothed.
explanation.definitionFit: A dressed wound is one that has had a protective wrapping or covering applied.

clue.text: Scottish jury in part of area, perhaps

parts.note: playing in the part of a character means acting as them
area is one measure of size

explanation.surface: A Scottish panel of jurors serving in some region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in part of' looks like a containment instruction, but it means 'as', as in playing the role of.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots law the word was used for a trial jury, as well as for a court sitting.

clue.text: Test papers? Test for one cabbie

parts.note: to test someone is to tax them, strain their patience
ID, identity documents, are papers
the Test is a river in Hampshire, England, famous for trout

explanation.surface: Questions about exam papers and the knowledge test a London taxi driver must pass.
explanation.walkthrough: Test appears twice with two jobs: a verb meaning tax, then the name of an English river.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabbie is informal for a person who drives a taxi for a living.

clue.text: Gangster, better one

parts.note: to better something is to cap or top it

explanation.surface: A mobster trying to outdo a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' is a verb here, to outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: Al Capone was the notorious Chicago mob boss of the Prohibition era.

clue.text: Suspended writer, awfully loud American

parts.note: a pen is a writing implement, a writer

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: An author with a terribly noisy American friend is banned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspended' suggests a ban but means hanging down; 'awfully' turns LOUD into DULO.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hanging loosely and swinging is described as hanging down, like a pendulum.

clue.text: Quandary — 'Birdsong', unfinished novel

indicators.note: unfinished means the last letter of the birdsong word is dropped

parts.note: a trill is a warbling birdsong
Emma is the Jane Austen novel

explanation.surface: A dilemma over two novels, Birdsong (by Sebastian Faulks) and one left incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Birdsong' is the title of a famous novel, but here it is simply a bird's song; 'unfinished' cuts TRILL to TRIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilemma has two unattractive options; this word extends the predicament to three choices.

clue.text: Ground cover often hides first of leaves

indicators.note: a word that hides another keeps it inside, so the second goes into the first

parts.note: much can mean often, as in 'do you go there much?'

indicators.note: first of means the opening letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Garden cover which commonly conceals the earliest fallen leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulch is a layer of compost or bark spread over soil to protect and enrich it.

clue.text: Huge prison in Palma?

definitions.note: describes someone or something found in Palma, so an adjective or noun of place

parts.note: major means great, huge
can is American slang for jail

explanation.surface: An enormous jail on a Mediterranean island.
explanation.walkthrough: Palma is the capital of the Spanish island of Majorca; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Palma is a native of the Balearic island where that city stands.

clue.text: Putrefaction in a seed plant

indicators.note: in places the decay word within the seed word

parts.note: a pea is a seed of the pea plant
rot is decay, putrefaction

explanation.surface: Decay setting in on some plant that grows from seed.
explanation.definitionFit: The protea is a South African flowering shrub with large showy blooms.

clue.text: Off road, jeep is put at risk

indicators.note: off suggests something wrong or out of place, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Taking a four-by-four off the tarmac endangers it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off road' looks like the familiar phrase, but 'Off' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger something is to expose it to danger or harm.

clue.text: Yearbook article in 25

indicators.note: in places the article within the word from the other clue

parts.note: the answer to 25 means release, cancel, which is to annul
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A yearbook with an entry printed in some other item.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference gives a synonym of the answer to 25, not its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A book published once a year, like a children's comic compilation, is called this.

clue.text: Drink with introverted guards

indicators.note: a word that guards another surrounds it, so the second goes inside

parts.note: introverted people are shy
and can mean with, as in 'fish and chips'

explanation.surface: Having a drink alongside some timid security staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, a popular British pub drink.

clue.text: More than happy with start of board game

indicators.note: start of means the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: lotto is a game of chance like bingo

explanation.surface: Glad to begin a board game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'happy' here is slang for tipsy, so 'more than happy' is very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Being well past merrily tipsy is to be completely drunk, in slang terms.

clue.text: One's very short but ultimately long

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: to long for something is to itch for it

explanation.surface: Someone tiny who is nonetheless tall in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'long' looks like the opposite of short but is a verb meaning yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a British nickname for a very small person or a child, a tiddler.

clue.text: Tragic hero's family belongings left inside

parts.note: kin are one's family

indicators.note: inside says the letter for left goes within the belongings word

parts.note: gear means one's possessions, belongings

explanation.surface: A heroic figure whose relatives keep his possessions indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Shakespeare's tragedy is the old king brought down by his own folly.

clue.text: Book about one prisoner's facial expression?

indicators.note: about means the book word is turned round

parts.note: a tome is a large book
I is the Roman numeral for one
con is short for convict, a prisoner

explanation.surface: A book about a convict's facial expressions.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that this face is a little keyboard symbol, not a real one.
explanation.definitionFit: A smiley or similar symbol typed into messages is a stylised face showing mood.

clue.text: Nessun Dorma's concealed release

indicators.note: concealed says the letters lie within the aria title, across its two words

explanation.surface: The famous Puccini aria was hiding its own release date.
explanation.definitionFit: To unfasten or free something is to release it, as with a knot or button.

clue.text: See whiskey bottles near wife

indicators.note: a word that bottles another holds it inside, so the pieces go within the whisky

parts.note: Bell's is a well-known brand of Scotch whisky
near means close by, at hand

explanation.surface: Look at whiskey bottles placed by your wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is not a verb but a noun, a bishop's diocese; Bath and Wells is one in Somerset, England.
explanation.definitionFit: The diocese of a bishop is called a see, and this one covers Somerset.
